entries.title: Reported: New would-be-final CLARITY Act draft circulated July 22 with DOJ-enforced ethics ban on federal officials issuing digital assets
entries.facts: As reported by CoinDesk on July 22, 2026 and corroborated by CNBC, Roll Call, American Banker and Disruption Banking the same day, lawmakers circulated a would-be-final draft of the Digital Asset Market CLARITY Act as the U.S. Senate prepared for floor action before its August recess. The draft includes a conflict-of-interest section barring the President, Vice President, members of Congress, federal judges and their spouses from issuing or sponsoring digital assets for pay while in office; per CNBC, the Department of Justice would enforce the ban with fines of up to $250,000 per day and disgorgement of profits plus a penalty of up to 10% of amounts received. The ethics provision is set to sunset January 20, 2029 and would require regulators to implement it within one year of enactment. Per CoinDesk, the draft retains the Blockchain Regulatory Certainty Act (non-custodial developers not treated as money transmitters) and adds new language on federal preemption, provisional registration and commodity pool operators. Senate Majority Leader John Thune's office said he intends to move to floor action in the coming days; the draft text was posted at Punchbowl News but had not been shared with Democratic lawmakers, several of whom criticized the DOJ-enforced ethics mechanism. The bill needs 60 Senate votes.
entries.source_label: CoinDesk, July 22, 2026 (corroborated by CNBC, Roll Call, American Banker, Disruption Banking)
entries.relevant_to: digital asset issuers, exchanges, DeFi developers, crypto compliance teams

entries.issuing_body: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (Commissioner Hester M. Peirce)
entries.title: SEC Commissioner Peirce: some crypto vaults and onchain lending strategies may fall within federal securities laws
entries.facts: On July 22, 2026, SEC Commissioner Hester M. Peirce issued a statement titled 'Headstands and Summervaults: A Statement on Crypto Vaults and Lending Strategies,' stating that crypto vaults and onchain lending strategies may fall within the federal securities laws depending on how they are structured and managed. Peirce wrote that moving activities within the scope of the securities laws onchain 'as a general matter, does not take those activities outside the scope,' and that 'tokenized securities are still securities. That principle holds for vaults.' She said parties who manage vaults (for example, by selecting yield-generating activities, re-allocating assets, or selecting the parties that make those decisions) or lending strategies (for example, by setting interest rates, deciding which assets to accommodate, and setting loan-to-value limits and liquidation thresholds) may want to analyze whether their activities implicate the securities laws; that a vault could be a common enterprise or fall into investment company territory and involvement may implicate investment adviser requirements; and that onchain loans could bear the hallmarks of notes that are securities. She stated the analysis turns on the specific facts and circumstances and invited market participants to engage with the SEC. The statement is an individual Commissioner statement, not a Commission rule or enforcement action.
entries.source_label: SEC.gov — Commissioner Hester M. Peirce statement, July 22, 2026
entries.relevant_to: DeFi vault operators and curators, onchain lending platforms, exchanges offering stablecoin yield
